title: Domain-driven design
subtitle: Learn how to keep code and business words in step, split a big model into bounded contexts, and draw aggregates around real rules, and when all of this is too much.

c.v: This story is made up, but each part is common. An online shop sells kitchenware. One
table serves the catalogue team, the billing team and the warehouse team. It has 64 columns and a flag called
The catalogue team wanted to reshoot photos of a popular steel bottle. So a developer set
to hide its page for a week. That was the meaning of "active" in catalogue code.
The warehouse restock job also read
. To the warehouse team, it meant "keep ordering this from the supplier". So the job stopped buying bottles.
The page came back a week later. Stock was nearly zero. Over the next weekend, 300 orders waited on bottles the shop did not have. Support spent days on apology emails.
Nobody wrote a bug. Each team used the word correctly, in its own sense. The code had one word for two different ideas.

Fowler describes DDD as building software around a domain model with "a rich understanding of the processes and rules of a domain".
The name comes from Eric Evans's 2003 book. Fowler says it fits complex domains with "a lot of often-messy logic".
Evans sums DDD up in three points. Focus on the core domain. Explore models together with business experts. And "speak a
DDD works at two levels. Evans says it "addresses both tactical and strategic design".
splits a large system into bounded contexts and maps how they relate.
gives you building blocks inside one context: entities,

One word should mean one thing inside one part of the system. Draw a boundary around each part, give it its own model, and translate where the parts meet. Inside each part, group objects around the business rules that must always hold.
Business experts and developers often use different words for the same things. Evans warns that the words of daily talk are often disconnected from the words in the code.
So the team agrees on one
. It is used in talk, in documents, and "in the code".
Evans adds that "a change in the language is a change to the model".
If the experts start saying "reserve stock", rename
. Experts should object to awkward terms, and developers should watch for unclear ones.

One language for the whole company does not work. Fowler saw the word "meter" mean subtly different things to different groups at a power company. He says the same confusion comes up again and again with "Customer" and "Product".
Fowler quotes Evans's book: "total unification of the domain model for a large system will not be feasible or cost-effective".
is a boundary, "typically a subsystem, or the work of a particular team", inside which one model applies.
Different contexts can model the same idea in completely different ways.
Microsoft's example: one person is a User in one service, a Buyer in another, a Payer in a third and a Customer in a fourth.
Step through the shop from the story. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
names each bounded context and its points of contact, with "explicit translation for any communication".
Evans lists common relationships. Three you will meet often:
Two teams share a small part of the model and its code. Keep it small. Neither team changes it without talking to the other.
One team depends on another. The downstream team's needs are part of the upstream team's planning.
You depend on a system whose model does not fit yours, such as a legacy app. You build a layer that translates its model into your own words.
has an identity that lasts while its data changes. An order is still the same order after its address changes. Evans says "the model must define what it means to be the same thing."
has no identity. You care only about its values, as with an amount of money.
To change one, you replace it with a new one.
Watch the words. Fowler notes that "entity" is often used to mean a database table, which is not the DDD sense.
An aggregate is "a cluster of domain objects that can be treated as a single unit", such as an order and its line items.
. Outside code holds references only to the root, and the root enforces the rules.
Apply rules synchronously inside the boundary and asynchronously across boundaries.
Vaughn Vernon shows why size matters. A Scrum tool modelled Product as one big aggregate holding all backlog items, releases and sprints.
Bill added a backlog item, and the Product version went up. Joe then scheduled a release. His save failed, because his copy was based on the old version.
No real rule linked the two changes. Vernon calls these "false invariants".
Model true invariants in consistency boundaries.
An invariant is a rule that must always be true. Only objects tied by such a rule belong in one aggregate.
On one project, about 70% of aggregates were just a root entity with some value properties.
He also says to change only one aggregate per
These are guidelines, not laws. He lists reasons to break them, such as batch screens or having no messaging system.

How do you pick? Vernon passes on a test from Evans. Is it the job of the user doing this action to make the data consistent? Then try to make it transactional, while still following the other aggregate rules. If it is another user's job, or the system's, let it be eventual.

It is usually immutable and often carries a timestamp and the IDs of the entities involved.

Bounded contexts are a good first guide to service boundaries. Microsoft notes that one bounded context may hold several services, "but not vice versa".
You chose well if typical operations rarely need data from several models.
A common trap is one service per table: Product, Customer, Order. Most features then need all three. Microsoft says that if two services must collaborate a lot, "they should probably be the same
Splitting along contexts, not tables, is the idea the
Microsoft says to use DDD only for "complex microservices with significant business rules". A CRUD service can stay simple.
It also notes that people find the patterns hard to learn. The important part is aligning code with the business and its words.
Fowler notes the book has "a reputation for being a hard book to read", but says it repays the effort.
A common mistake is the opposite of skipping DDD: using every tactical pattern in a simple app, and skipping the talks with experts.
Evans himself says to spend the best effort on the core domain. For generic parts, he suggests off-the-shelf solutions.

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: When a meeting gets confused, ask:
"Which team's meaning of this word are we using?"
Keep a short glossary per context in the repo. Rename code when the business words change.
Before you add a field to a shared table, ask which contexts read it, and whether they read it the same way.
When you design an aggregate, list its true invariants first. If you cannot name one rule that links two objects, keep them apart.
If a use case changes two aggregates in one transaction, ask whose job the consistency is. Most of the time, an event will do.
Draw the context map before you draw the service map.
Skip the tactical patterns for CRUD screens. Spend the effort where the business makes its money.
"List every place in this codebase that reads or writes the products.active column. For each one, say in one line what the code assumes 'active' means."
"Here are three of our team glossaries. Find words that appear in more than one, and show where the meanings differ."

"This Order class is saved with its customer and every product in one transaction. List the business rules it enforces. For each rule, say which objects it really needs. Suggest smaller aggregates that reference others by ID."
The agent's rules came from the code or from experts, not from its guesses about your business.
Each proposed aggregate protects at least one real invariant. It is not just a group of related tables.

q.v: Sales, billing and shipping all use the word “customer”, but each needs different fields. What does DDD suggest?

options.v: One Customer class with every field, shared by all three teams.
A separate model in each bounded context, linked by the customer's ID, with translation where they meet.
Rename the word everywhere to “user” so there is no confusion.

why.v: Evans's book, quoted by Fowler, says one model for a large system is not feasible or cost-effective. Each bounded context keeps its own model, and you map between them where they connect.

q.v: Which of these is best modelled as a value object?

options.v: A customer, who can change their name and address.
An order, which moves from draft to placed to shipped.
An amount of money, such as ₹499.00.

why.v: You care only about the amount and the currency. Two equal amounts are the same, and you replace a value instead of changing it. A customer and an order keep an identity while they change.

q.v: In Vernon's Scrum example, why did Joe's save fail after Bill added a backlog item?

options.v: Both changes went through one large Product aggregate, so optimistic concurrency rejected Joe's save as stale.
The database ran out of connections.
Joe broke a real business rule about releases.

why.v: Bill's commit raised the Product version. Joe's change was based on the old version, so it was rejected. The rule it protected was false. Planning an item and scheduling a release do not conflict.

q.v: When a customer places an order, your system must also reduce their loyalty points, which live in another aggregate. What do Vernon's rules suggest?

options.v: Load both aggregates and change them in one transaction.
Merge Order and LoyaltyAccount into one large aggregate.
Save the order, publish an OrderPlaced event, and update the points in a separate transaction.

why.v: Change one aggregate per transaction. Rules that span aggregates use eventual consistency, often through a domain event.

q.v: Your team plans to split a monolith into a Product service, a Customer service and an Order service, one per main table. What is the main risk?

options.v: The services will be too small to run in containers.
Most features need data from several of them, so the services become chatty and must change together.
Each service will need its own programming language.

why.v: Splitting by table ignores how the business works. Microsoft notes that if two services must collaborate a lot, they should probably be one service.
